name: Crocus Martis
lede: Crocus martis is an old name for an artificial iron oxide, made by burning iron, that painters and polishers used as a red or, in some recipes, a yellow.

sections.title: What it was
sections.body:
Pigment Compendium describes crocus martis as essentially a synthetic iron oxide, prepared by calcining iron sulfate [1]. Ball says medieval alchemists made an ochre-tinted product by oxidizing iron in air and called it crocus martis, a literal Latin rendering of Mars yellow [2].

The books disagree on the color. Ball notes that Sir Theodore de Mayerne, physician at the court of Charles I, gave the first artist's recipe he knows of, in an early seventeenth-century manuscript, and that de Mayerne's product is red [2]. De Mayerne gave three methods, among them calcining steel filings or iron chips in a furnace [1][2]. A later entry in the same compendium ties the crocus or saffron of Mars to a yellow, with patents of 1780 and 1794 marking the earliest period it was made [3]. So the name has covered both reds and yellows.

sections.title: Among the artificial reds
sections.body: The compendium groups it with Venetian red, Indian red, Tuscan red, light red, rouge, colcothar and caput mortuum, terms generally applied to synthetic iron reds [4]. Paterson lists crocus martis as another name for jeweller's rouge, a powdered red oxide used to polish gold and silver [5]. Paterson also says Mars colors are synthetic iron oxides, running through orange, black, brown and yellow [6]. Compare [[venetian-red]] and [[indian-red]].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch on this page is a muted greyish rose-brown, which comes from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930, the earliest record of the name in our sources [7]. It is paler and greyer than a strong iron-oxide red, and nearer to [[rosy-brown]] or [[dusty-rose]] in feel [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color appears in 211 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, as photographed [8]. Its most devoted painter is Maurice Denis, with 4 of his 43 works here, 5.4 times the baseline [8]. It is most over-represented in France, at 2.4 times the expected rate [8]. The earliest match is dated 1340, 590 years before the name's first record [8]. That is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the pigment [8].

origin.named_after: Latin crocus, saffron, and Mars, the old name for iron
origin.first_recorded: alchemical; as an artist's recipe, de Mayerne, early 17th century

disambiguation.gloss: Unrelated: crocus here means saffron-colored, not the flower
